picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Works out 4+ times a week and has direct supplements and recovery affinities, so pre-workout, creatine and protein are already a recurring purchase. Price sensitivity low-medium means they'll switch only if performance is equal \u2014 which is exactly the brand's 'same formulations' claim.
lean_into: same dose, same actives as the expensive tubs
built for people who train 4-5x a week
avoid: athlete endorsements the brand can't back
picks.ad_angle: Same formulations as the brand you're already using \u2014 read the label, then look at the price.

picks.name: The Value-Conscious Shopper
picks.why_plausible: price_sensitivity: high, comparison shops, reads reviews and responds to 'clear value props' and 'bundle offers' \u2014 which is literally the brand's only pitch (half the cost). Score ranked them mid because their affinities are grocery/household, but supplements are a replenishment staple bought the same way: by unit price.
lean_into: clear value props: half the price of the big names
picks.ad_angle: Do the math: cost per serving versus the name brand, side by side.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Tracks supplements and workouts, with supplements and fitness among her top affinities \u2014 creatine and protein are core to her optimization stack. Score flagged a price mismatch (price_sensitivity: low), but paying less for an identical ingredient panel is still a rational win for someone who reads labels.
lean_into: ingredient transparency \u2014 full label, no proprietary blends
honest comparison of actives against premium brands
avoid: claiming clinical trials the brand hasn't run
picks.ad_angle: Compare the ingredient panels \u2014 you're paying premium prices for the same actives.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Urban millennial who buys on replenishment autopilot and has low brand loyalty when something else is just as easy \u2014 an easy swap on a protein tub that runs out monthly. Score is low only because their affinities are delivery/subscription categories, but the swap-and-restock behavior is the exact buying motion here.
lean_into: frictionless reorder of the staple you already buy
low brand loyalty rewarded: same product, easy switch
picks.ad_angle: Your protein tub is almost empty \u2014 restock the same thing for half, in one tap.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Dual-income parent, buys in bulk, medium price sensitivity, and dislikes luxury positioning \u2014 a household where one or both adults train and the supplement line item recurs monthly. The score caught the replenishment and value fit; the specific reason is bulk-buying a recurring household cost down.
lean_into: clear family budget savings on a monthly cost
picks.ad_angle: Cut a recurring monthly household expense in half without changing what you buy.

plan.summary: Budget leans on the two genuine fitness moments — Movewell activewear and Studiogrid class/PT bookings — with tests on Swiftcart (young, male-leaning, impulse traffic at huge scale), Cloudfoot and Pop & Sip, while Daily Form is pulled out as a direct supplement competitor and Pantrygood dropped because its clean-claim audience rewards everything this brand doesn't sell on.

recommended.name: Studiogrid
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a generic wellness match, but the purchase moment is the sharpest in the catalog: someone who just booked a fitness class or personal training session is actively training, and pre-workout/protein is the natural next purchase at an almost identical basket size ($40 vs $42).
recommended.rationale: Notes say "Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness" and the site sells personal training and fitness classes, so the offer lands on someone with a training session literally on the calendar, at a matching price point.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: Spa and yoga bookings dilute the lifter signal, and a high-income 74%-female audience may not be the price-shopping creatine buyer the brand targets.

recommended.name: Movewell
recommended.rationale: Notes describe "Fitness-engaged shoppers" buying activewear on subscription, so a $40 restock of protein/creatine is an easy add-on to a $78 gym-kit basket.
recommended.risk: 82% female, mid-high income audience skews toward wellness/beauty crossover rather than lifters buying pre-workout and creatine, and budget positioning is a weaker hook at this income tier.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.tier_reason: Off-category is right about the basket but misses that this is the only place the advertiser's stated buyer profile appears at scale: 18-34, 51% male, mid income, impulse-friendly, and a $28 basket that makes a $40 value offer a small step up.
test.rationale: Worth a read purely on audience and volume: "High-frequency purchasers... Impulse-friendly" young mid-income men at 84M impressions is the cheapest way to test whether a price-led supplement offer converts on impulse traffic.

evidence.quote: High-frequency purchasers. Late-night traffic spike. Impulse-friendly

test.risk: No fitness intent in the basket at all; late-night convenience and alcohol orders may convert poorly despite the demographic match.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.rationale: Sells activewear and footwear to a 25-45 mixed-gender audience, so there is a plausible training-adjacent buyer, but notes frame it as "Tech-adjacent urban professionals. Comfort + sustainability messaging" rather than performance.

evidence.quote: Tech-adjacent urban professionals. Comfort + sustainability messaging

test.risk: Comfort-shoe buyers at a $118 basket may be lifestyle rather than gym buyers, and the sustainability-led sensibility does not reward a price-only pitch.

test.name: Pop & Sip
test.rationale: Functional-beverage and gut-health buyers already pay for ingestible wellness at a $42 basket that matches the offer, so the test is whether that habit extends to protein and creatine.
test.risk: Notes call the audience "Health-curious but indulgence-seeking" and 71% female; soda-alternative buyers are not necessarily training and may never buy pre-workout.

excluded.name: Kitchenly
excluded.rationale: Family meal-kit buyers are convenience-motivated; no link to gym supplement replenishment.

excluded.rationale: Bedding buyers at a $164 basket have no fitness purchase signal.

excluded.rationale: "Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims" are a poor match for a brand whose only claims are price and matching formulations, and an $86 organic grocery order says nothing about training.

evidence.quote: Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

excluded.rationale: Direct supplement seller, and its "Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims" is the worst possible fit for a same-formulation-for-half-price pitch.

assumptions: Assumed a first order around $40 based on half-price positioning.
Assumed a broad adult gym audience with no gender skew.
Assumed one-time purchases since no subscription was mentioned.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.

launch_summary.summary: Most of the $10,000 goes to two real fitness moments: Studiogrid class and PT bookings at $4,485.93 and Movewell activewear at $4,014.07, where all five personas run. A $1,500 test budget splits evenly across Swiftcart, Cloudfoot and Pop & Sip to learn whether a price-led supplement pitch converts on high-volume impulse traffic, comfort-led apparel buyers and functional-beverage buyers. Target cost per new customer is $12.00, with $15.60 as the ceiling during the 14-day learning period.
uncertainties: The $40 first order is inferred from half-price positioning, and the $12.00 target cost per new customer is built directly on it.
One-time purchasing is assumed since no subscription was mentioned, so repeat revenue isn't credited to the acquisition cost even though these products are replenishment buys.
The broad 20-40 adult gym audience with no gender skew is assumed, which matters most for Pop & Sip, whose audience is noted as 71% female and indulgence-seeking rather than training.
questions: What is the actual average first order value and gross margin on it?
Do you offer a subscription or see meaningful repeat purchases we should price acquisition against?
Does your buyer base skew male or to a narrower age band than 20-40?
